title: Finishing a tractate
hook: a celebration when a tractate is completed

segments.voice: Yesterday, still arguing: for the sake of heaven, Hillel's and Shammai's houses kept disagreeing and kept marrying each other. Did you say someone's point back to them before making yours? Day one thousand one hundred nineteen.

The last line of a tractate. Someone reads it aloud, slowly, and the room that has been quiet for an hour suddenly isn't. A cake appears from somewhere. Someone pours a drink. Someone else stands up to say a few words about the final page, and gets interrupted, and starts again. Months of study, sometimes years, one page at a time, and now the book is closed. It is not a quiet moment. It's a party. Today's word is the name of that party.
screen: `THE LAST LINE, READ ALOUD.` → `A CAKE APPEARS.` → `A BOOK CLOSES. A PARTY STARTS.`

segments.voice: Siyum. Completion, and the celebration that marks it. Turn it four ways. First, an old feast. The Talmud, in tractate Shabbat, tells of the sage Abaye saying that whenever he saw a young scholar finish a tractate, he made a feast for the rabbis. Notice whose finish it was. Not his own. He threw the party for somebody else's last page. Second, what's said. At a siyum, those who finished say a short traditional text called the hadran. It speaks to the tractate itself, by name, as if to a friend: we will return to you, and you will return to us. We won't forget you, and you won't forget us. The ending is not goodbye. It's see you again. Third, the meal. The celebration meal after a siyum is treated as a seudat mitzvah, a meal that is itself part of a commandment, like the meal at a wedding or a circumcision. And there's a custom that grows out of that. On the day before Passover, by custom, firstborns fast. Some attend a siyum that morning, and joining its meal releases them from the fast. Fourth, the size. A siyum can be three people around a kitchen table who finished a small tractate together, or a crowd in a large hall when a daily study cycle reaches the end of the whole Talmud. Same words, same promise to return. The siyum.
screen: `ABAYE'S FEAST FOR SOMEONE ELSE.` · `WE WILL RETURN TO YOU.` · `A MEAL THAT IS A COMMANDMENT.` · `A KITCHEN TABLE OR A GREAT HALL.` · then, large: `THE SIYUM.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to celebrate finishing one thing. Settle, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind something you finished recently. A project. A book. A hard week. A course of treatment. A long-overdue phone call. Let yourself see the last page of it. Don't judge how well it went. The siyum marks reaching the end, not doing it perfectly. Now, quietly, tell it what the hadran tells a tractate: I'll come back to you. Then think of one small way to mark it today. The bell holds the time.
Siyum. Completion: the celebration when a tractate, or another unit of study, is finished, with the hadran's promise to return. Today's word.
Your line: the siyum. Today, mark one finish, yours or someone else's, the way Abaye did: with food, a toast, or just a few words out loud. Day one thousand one hundred nineteen.

howItsDone: When a person or group completes a tractate, they hold a siyum: the last passage is read, the hadran is recited, someone teaches a few words on the tractate, and a festive meal follows. A siyum is often held on the morning before Passover so that firstborns may join the meal.
